invariants: Local authentication can never be disabled; it is the fallback that keeps the product administrable.
No recoverable password exists anywhere in the product.
A refusal never reveals whether an identity exists.
No credential material reaches an audit row, a log line or an error message.
Sessions, RBAC and audit stay exactly as C3 fixes them.
Identity is owned by the service, never by a proxy in front of it.
Changing a password is possible from the first release; only the compulsion to change is deferred, and the deferral is recorded as a dated Product Owner decision with a revisit condition.
Agent actions are attributable to the agent's own identity, never merged with a human administrator's.

requirements: English, per AGENTS.md engineering-output language law.
This movement produces ONE document. No source file is created or changed.
The document's status is DRAFT -- NOT implementation authority. Applying a status is the Product Owner's act, not this movement's. Say so in the status block.
Every rule must be traceable to measured behaviour or to a FROZEN document, and must carry a check. A rule with no check is a wish.
Where something is not settled, write UNKNOWN with what would settle it. AGENTS.md forbids filling a gap from general product knowledge.
Do not merge to main. The Product Owner assistant reviews the diff and merges.
Do not run the full pytest suite. It creates untracked data/ and logs/ directories the privacy gate then flags.
No real identity -- no serial, hostname, address, domain, certificate subject or display name -- may appear in the document.

Where this contract and a FROZEN document are in tension -- the Ingress question is one -- report the tension explicitly with both citations, and leave it for the Product Owner. AGENTS.md 'Authority hierarchy': never silently reconcile two authorities.
risks: Designing an elaborate password policy nobody asked for.
Redesigning sessions or RBAC, which C3 already owns and this contract must leave alone.
Silently resolving the Ingress tension instead of reporting it.
Putting identity in the proxy because it is convenient.
Designing LDAP detail, which is out of scope and already owned.
Letting a verifier, a salt or a parameter set appear in an audit row.

Re-arguing the forced-password-change decision instead of recording it. The Product Owner heard the risk and decided; this contract records the decision, the risk and the revisit condition, and does not re-litigate.
Writing a password policy the Product Owner explicitly deferred.

in: The mechanism registry: authentication is a set, local is a member, and local can never be removed or disabled. State how a mechanism is selected for an attempt and how the outcome is reported, so that adding LDAP later is adding a member and not rewriting the flow. C3's Correction C-2 is the authority; this section makes it concrete.

Local credential storage. The stored value must be a one-way verifier produced by a memory-hard password hashing function with a per-credential salt -- never a reversible encryption, never a plain or merely digested password. Name the algorithm family and the parameters that must be recorded alongside each verifier so parameters can be raised later without invalidating existing credentials. State explicitly that no product table ever holds a recoverable password, consistent with UI2_0_B1_04B section 6's rule for device credentials.

The bootstrap accounts. TWO accounts exist on a clean, empty database: `nexusadmin` and `claudeadmin`. `claudeadmin` is the assistant's own account and exists so that actions taken by the automation are attributable to it rather than to the Product Owner -- state that audit benefit explicitly, because it is the reason the second account is worth having at all. **A forced password change is NOT required at this stage.** The Product Owner ruled on 2026-09-13 that password-policy standards are later work and declined the forced change after being told the risk. Record that decision as the Product Owner's, with its date and its stated reason, and record the risk plainly alongside it: a bootstrap credential that survives onto a reachable server is the product's weakest point. Give the risk a named REVISIT CONDITION rather than an argument -- the forced change, or an equivalent, is required before the surface is reachable from outside the server or before any production deployment, whichever comes first. Changing a password must be POSSIBLE from the first release; it is only the compulsion that is deferred.

Login behaviour and lockout: failed-attempt counting, the threshold, what the lockout does, how it clears, and what the response says. The response must not reveal whether an identity exists -- a refusal is a refusal. Fix whether lockout is per identity, per source, or both, and say why.
Password change and password rules: what the product requires of a new password, stated as checkable rules. Keep them defensible and few; do not invent an elaborate policy.

RBAC in the local mechanism: C3 already owns the RBAC model and it is mechanism-independent. State only how a LOCAL identity acquires its role binding, and record the Product Owner's forward requirement that distinct teams will hold distinct roles -- one seeing failover, another configuration -- so the model must already represent that even while only one account exists.

Audit: every authentication attempt, lockout, password change and role binding change is audited through C1 section 3.5's existing mechanism. No credential, no verifier, no salt and no parameter set ever reaches an audit row, a log line or an error message.

Exposure: record the Product Owner's 2026-09-13 directive that no screen is exposed outside the server, and state the consequence for this contract -- the login surface is reachable in-cluster only. Note that docs/design/UI2_0_B1_01C_CONTAINER_IMAGE_AND_KUBERNETES_DEPLOYMENT_CONTRACT.md defines an Ingress, that this directive is in tension with it, and REPORT the tension rather than resolving it: AGENTS.md forbids silently reconciling two authorities.

A section stating what a reverse proxy may and may not do: it may terminate TLS; it may not own identity. Give the reason from C3 -- the one-active-session-per-identity rule and the audit trail both require the service to know who authenticated, which an upstream proxy performing the authentication would take away.
Acceptance criteria and a test specification, including the forced-bootstrap-change test and a test that no credential material appears in any audit row or log line.
out: Any implementation, Java, SQL, migration or screen. This movement writes one document.
LDAP, RADIUS or TACACS mechanism detail. C3 owns LDAP; RADIUS and TACACS are named by C-2 as later and nothing may be designed for them here. This contract only ensures the registry admits them.
Changing anything C3 already fixes about sessions, RBAC or audit. They are mechanism-independent and unchanged.
Changing the C1 schema contract, the deployment contract, or any other FROZEN document. Report a tension; never resolve it here.
Designing the user-management screens. State what the mechanism requires; the screen is a separate contract.
Self-service password reset, email flows, multi-factor, or session-token cryptography. C3 owns sessions.

Designing a password-policy standard -- complexity classes, expiry, history, reuse rules. The Product Owner explicitly deferred this on 2026-09-13. State only the minimum a new password must satisfy to be storable, and nothing about policy.
